entry_json.definition: spoken question asking how someone is managing or progressing; it almost always appears inside the longer frame 'How are you getting on (with sth)?'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: How are you getting on with your new course?
example_sentences: Are you getting on all right with the new system at work?
Are you getting on with the reading list, or has it defeated you?

contexts.text: How are you getting on with your new course?
Are you getting on all right with the new system at work?
Are you getting on with the reading list, or has it defeated you?

confusables.difference: 'How are you?' asks about health or mood. 'How are you getting on?' asks about progress with a particular task, so it needs a with-phrase or an obvious situation.
The same three words change meaning with the object: 'get on with sb' is about relationships, 'get on with sth' is about progress.

entry_json.avoid: Spoken only. In Task 2 write 'is progressing' or 'is coping with' instead.

entry_json.definition: question frame asking whether something has happened at any time in someone's life up to now; the verb after it must be a past participle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Have you ever travelled abroad on your own?
example_sentences: Have you ever tried cooking a dish from another country?
Have you ever had a job that changed the way you think about money?

contexts.text: Have you ever travelled abroad on your own?
Have you ever tried cooking a dish from another country?
Have you ever had a job that changed the way you think about money?

confusables.difference: 'Have you ever…?' covers your whole life up to now. 'Did you ever…?' points at a finished period, such as your school years.
'Do you ever…?' asks how often something happens. 'Have you ever…?' asks whether it has happened at all.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'Have you ever went'. The verb has to be a past participle: been, gone, tried, seen.

entry_json.definition: spoken frame for making a suggestion or asking someone's view; followed by a noun or an -ing form, never a to-infinitive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: How about cycling to work instead of driving?
example_sentences: How about a weekend in the mountains, if the weather holds?
Exams cause a lot of stress, in my view. How about you?

contexts.text: How about cycling to work instead of driving?
How about a weekend in the mountains, if the weather holds?
Exams cause a lot of stress, in my view. How about you?

confusables.difference: Nearly interchangeable as suggestions, but 'What about…?' is the one that raises an objection nobody has considered - 'What about the cost?' - while 'How about…?' mainly proposes.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'How about to go'. Use the -ing form: 'How about going?'

entry_json.definition: the standard spoken greeting asking about someone's health or general state; it works as a greeting rather than a real question, so a short answer is expected
entry_json.own_context_sentence: How are you? I haven't seen you since the summer.
example_sentences: How are you? Sorry to keep you waiting - the meeting overran.
A quick 'How are you?' in the corridor is a greeting, not a question about anybody's health.

contexts.text: How are you? I haven't seen you since the summer.
How are you? Sorry to keep you waiting - the meeting overran.
A quick 'How are you?' in the corridor is a greeting, not a question about anybody's health.

confusables.difference: 'How do you do?' is a very formal first-meeting greeting and is now rare. 'How are you?' is the everyday one.
That asks about progress with something specific; 'How are you?' asks about the person.

entry_json.avoid: A spoken greeting only. It has no place in an essay, and the examiner does not want a medical history in reply.

entry_json.definition: question frame asking about duration; the answer is a period of time, and with a present perfect it asks how long a situation has lasted so far
entry_json.own_context_sentence: How long have you lived in this part of the city?
example_sentences: How long did it take you to get used to studying in English?
How long a commute is reasonable before people start moving out of the city?

contexts.text: How long have you lived in this part of the city?
How long did it take you to get used to studying in English?
How long a commute is reasonable before people start moving out of the city?

confusables.difference: 'How long…?' asks about time; 'How far…?' asks about distance. 'How long is the journey?' can be read either way, so add 'in hours' if it matters.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'How long time…?' - the word 'long' already carries the idea of time.

entry_json.definition: question frame asking about quantity with countable plural nouns: 'How many hours…?', 'How many students…?'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: How many hours a week do you spend studying outside class?
example_sentences: The table shows how many households moved into rented accommodation after 2010.
How many people actually change their diet after a warning like that?

contexts.text: How many hours a week do you spend studying outside class?
The table shows how many households moved into rented accommodation after 2010.
How many people actually change their diet after a warning like that?

confusables.difference: 'How many' goes with countable plurals - how many students. 'How much' goes with uncountables - how much time, how much money.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'How many informations' or 'How many advices'. Those nouns are uncountable and take 'how much'.

entry_json.definition: question frame asking about an amount of something uncountable, or about price: 'How much water…?', 'How much is it?'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: How much do you usually spend on transport in a month?
example_sentences: How much time did you give yourself to prepare for the test?
The real question is how much responsibility the individual should carry for their own health.

contexts.text: How much do you usually spend on transport in a month?
How much time did you give yourself to prepare for the test?
The real question is how much responsibility the individual should carry for their own health.

confusables.difference: 'How much' is for uncountables and prices; 'How many' is for things you can count one by one.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'How much books'. If you can put a number in front of the noun, you need 'how many'.

entry_json.definition: question frame asking about frequency; the answer is an expression of frequency such as 'twice a week', not a length of time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: How often do you do any kind of exercise during the week?
example_sentences: How often do you read the news in English?
How often the buses run matters more to passengers than how fast they are.
collocations: How often should sb do sth?

contexts.text: How often do you do any kind of exercise during the week?
How often do you read the news in English?
How often the buses run matters more to passengers than how fast they are.

confusables.difference: 'How often…?' asks about a habit and expects 'twice a week'. 'How many times…?' counts occasions inside a finished period - 'How many times did you take the test?'

entry_json.avoid: Answer it with a frequency, not a duration: 'twice a month', not 'for two hours'.

entry_json.definition: spoken filler used while you look for a tactful or precise way to say something; it buys thinking time and warns the listener that what follows is being softened
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My first manager was, how shall I put it, not very interested in training anybody.
example_sentences: The new development is - how shall I put it? - not to everybody's taste.
It was, how shall I put it, a rather generous interpretation of the rules.

contexts.text: My first manager was, how shall I put it, not very interested in training anybody.
The new development is - how shall I put it? - not to everybody's taste.
It was, how shall I put it, a rather generous interpretation of the rules.

confusables.difference: 'How shall I put it?' is the fixed English form. 'How shall I say?' is a direct translation from other languages and sounds wrong.
'I mean' repairs something you have already said. 'How shall I put it?' delays what you are about to say while you find a polite word.

entry_json.avoid: Spoken only, and once per answer. Written down it is padding; repeated it sounds evasive.

entry_json.definition: spoken frame that either suggests something or raises a point the other person has left out; followed by a noun or an -ing form
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Everyone talks about recycling, but what about the packaging in the first place?
example_sentences: What about visiting the museum while entry is still free?
What about families who simply cannot afford the equipment?

contexts.text: Everyone talks about recycling, but what about the packaging in the first place?
What about visiting the museum while entry is still free?
What about families who simply cannot afford the equipment?

confusables.difference: Both make suggestions, but only 'What about…?' comfortably raises an objection: 'What about the people who work nights?'

entry_json.avoid: Not 'What about to visit'. The verb takes -ing: 'What about visiting…?'

entry_json.definition: spoken question asking what is happening, usually when a situation is confusing or something seems wrong
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I walked into the office and everyone was packing boxes, so I asked what's going on.
example_sentences: Younger people follow several apps just to know what's going on in their own city.
Neighbours who know each other notice when something is wrong and ask what's going on.

contexts.text: I walked into the office and everyone was packing boxes, so I asked what's going on.
Younger people follow several apps just to know what's going on in their own city.
Neighbours who know each other notice when something is wrong and ask what's going on.

confusables.difference: 'What happened?' asks about a finished event. 'What's going on?' asks about a situation that is still unfolding.
'What is the matter?' assumes there is a problem with a person. 'What's going on?' is neutral about who is involved.

entry_json.avoid: Informal and spoken. In writing use 'what is happening' or 'the current situation'.

entry_json.definition: spoken frame for suggesting something, followed by the bare infinitive - 'Why not ask?' - or used on its own to agree to a suggestion
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Why not walk the last stop instead of taking the bus the whole way?
example_sentences: If the course is free, why not try it for a term?
Why not open the museums late one evening a week?

contexts.text: Why not walk the last stop instead of taking the bus the whole way?
If the course is free, why not try it for a term?
Why not open the museums late one evening a week?

confusables.difference: 'Why don't you…?' points at one person. 'Why not…?' is impersonal and can propose something for everybody, which suits Part 3.
'Why?' asks for a reason. 'Why not…?' does not really ask anything - it proposes.

entry_json.avoid: Bare infinitive after it: 'Why not go?', never 'Why not to go?'

entry_json.definition: polite spoken offer or invitation, followed by a noun or a to-infinitive; the standard reply is 'Yes, please' or 'No, thank you'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Would you like something to drink before we start?
example_sentences: Would you like to come with us to the coast at the weekend?
Would you like to work from home permanently, or would two days be enough?

contexts.text: Would you like something to drink before we start?
Would you like to come with us to the coast at the weekend?
Would you like to work from home permanently, or would two days be enough?

confusables.difference: Same meaning, different politeness. 'Do you want…?' is fine with friends; 'Would you like…?' is what you use with a stranger, a customer or an examiner.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'Would you like drinking?' - it takes 'to drink'. And do not answer with 'Yes, I would like'.

entry_json.definition: a small amount; placed before an adjective or adverb it softens what you are saying - 'a bit tired'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was a bit nervous before my first seminar in English.
example_sentences: The flat is a bit small, but the location makes up for it.
Working from home is a bit lonely if you live on your own.

contexts.text: I was a bit nervous before my first seminar in English.
The flat is a bit small, but the location makes up for it.
Working from home is a bit lonely if you live on your own.

confusables.difference: Both soften, but 'a bit' is spoken and usually attaches to a negative adjective - a bit boring, a bit expensive. 'A little' is neutral and safer in writing.
'A bit' modifies adjectives; 'a bit of sth' takes a noun. 'A bit tired' but 'a bit of luck'.

entry_json.avoid: Too informal for Task 2. Write 'slightly' or 'somewhat' instead.

entry_json.definition: a slightly larger amount or degree; used before a comparative adjective or before a noun - 'a bit more time'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I just needed a bit more time to finish the reading before the seminar.
example_sentences: People are willing to pay a bit more for food that is grown locally.
If schools gave children a bit more space to play, fitness would improve on its own.

contexts.text: I just needed a bit more time to finish the reading before the seminar.
People are willing to pay a bit more for food that is grown locally.
If schools gave children a bit more space to play, fitness would improve on its own.

confusables.difference: The same shape but a very different size. 'A bit more' is a small increase, 'a lot more' a large one - choose deliberately when you describe a chart.

entry_json.avoid: Informal. When describing a graph, write 'slightly higher' rather than 'a bit more'.

entry_json.definition: spoken softener placed before a noun, meaning something is rather that thing; it usually plays the situation down
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Getting to campus in winter is a bit of a nightmare.
example_sentences: My first month in the job was a bit of a struggle, to be honest.
Finding somewhere affordable near the centre is a bit of a lottery.

contexts.text: Getting to campus in winter is a bit of a nightmare.
My first month in the job was a bit of a struggle, to be honest.
Finding somewhere affordable near the centre is a bit of a lottery.

confusables.difference: 'A bit of sth' is a genuine small quantity - a bit of bread. 'A bit of a…' is not about quantity at all; it labels something, normally to understate it.

entry_json.avoid: British spoken English. In an essay write 'something of a problem', or simply name the problem.

entry_json.definition: a small amount of something uncountable; the pattern is a bit of + uncountable noun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I do a bit of revision on the train every morning.
example_sentences: With a bit of luck the scholarship will cover most of the fees.
A bit of exercise every day does more good than one hard session a week.

contexts.text: I do a bit of revision on the train every morning.
With a bit of luck the scholarship will cover most of the fees.
A bit of exercise every day does more good than one hard session a week.

confusables.difference: 'A bit of' takes uncountable nouns - a bit of information. 'A few' takes countable plurals - a few facts.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a bit of books'. If the noun has a plural form, use 'a few'.

entry_json.definition: two, or a small number close to two; it takes a plural countable noun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I take a couple of online courses alongside my degree.
example_sentences: We stayed a couple of nights in a hostel to keep the cost down.
Sales fell for a couple of years before recovering in 2015.

contexts.text: I take a couple of online courses alongside my degree.
We stayed a couple of nights in a hostel to keep the cost down.
Sales fell for a couple of years before recovering in 2015.

confusables.difference: 'A couple of' means two, or very nearly two. 'A few' is vaguer - roughly three to five.

entry_json.avoid: Fairly informal. If the chart gives you the figure, write 'two' rather than 'a couple of'.

entry_json.definition: one or two days; a deliberately vague short period used when you do not want to promise an exact time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The manager said the decision would take a day or two.
example_sentences: I felt tired for a day or two after the flight, and then I was fine.
People expect a reply within a day or two now, which adds real pressure at work.

contexts.text: The manager said the decision would take a day or two.
I felt tired for a day or two after the flight, and then I was fine.
People expect a reply within a day or two now, which adds real pressure at work.

confusables.difference: The same length of time, a different attitude. 'A couple of days' states it; 'a day or two' leaves room to be wrong.

entry_json.avoid: The pattern is fixed: 'a day or two', never 'one or two day'.

entry_json.definition: a fall in how many students there are; a fixed academic collocation built on decline in + plural noun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The graph shows a decline in student numbers at rural schools between 2005 and 2020.
example_sentences: A decline in student numbers forces small universities either to merge or to close.
A decline in student numbers is not always bad news if class sizes improve.
collocations: a sharp decline in student numbers
a steady decline in student numbers

contexts.text: The graph shows a decline in student numbers at rural schools between 2005 and 2020.
A decline in student numbers forces small universities either to merge or to close.
A decline in student numbers is not always bad news if class sizes improve.

confusables.difference: Interchangeable in most sentences, but 'decline' suggests a longer and more worrying trend, while 'decrease' is purely numerical.
The preposition is fixed: a decline IN something, never a decline OF it.

entry_json.avoid: Write 'a decline in student numbers', never 'a decline of student numbers'.

entry_json.definition: something wonderful that you had hoped for without really expecting; it works as a noun phrase after the verb 'be'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Playing in that stadium was a dream come true for him.
example_sentences: Studying abroad was a dream come true, although the first term was hard.
For most people a job they genuinely enjoy is a dream come true rather than a plan.
collocations: a dream come true for sb

contexts.text: Playing in that stadium was a dream come true for him.
Studying abroad was a dream come true, although the first term was hard.
For most people a job they genuinely enjoy is a dream come true rather than a plan.

confusables.difference: The fixed phrase keeps the bare form: 'It was a dream come true'. 'My dream came true' is a full sentence, not this phrase.

entry_json.avoid: Heavily overused in Speaking Part 2. Once is fine; it is not band-8 vocabulary by itself.

entry_json.definition: a small number of countable things, usually three to five; the tone is positive - it says there are some
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have a few friends who are taking the test in the same month.
example_sentences: A few countries have banned the advertising of sugary drinks to children.
Only a few employers offer proper training, and that is the real problem.

contexts.text: I have a few friends who are taking the test in the same month.
A few countries have banned the advertising of sugary drinks to children.
Only a few employers offer proper training, and that is the real problem.

confusables.difference: 'A few' means some. 'Few' without the article means almost none and sounds negative: 'Few students attended' is a complaint.
'A few' counts separate things; 'a little' measures something uncountable.

entry_json.avoid: Dropping 'a' reverses the meaning, so check which one you mean before you write it.

entry_json.definition: a short period of several minutes; the standard way to describe a brief wait or a quick task
entry_json.own_context_sentence: You get a few minutes to plan before you start speaking in Part 2.
example_sentences: The train was only a few minutes late, so it did not really matter.
Even a few minutes of walking each hour reduces the harm of sitting all day.

contexts.text: You get a few minutes to plan before you start speaking in Part 2.
The train was only a few minutes late, so it did not really matter.
Even a few minutes of walking each hour reduces the harm of sitting all day.

confusables.difference: Almost the same. 'A few minutes' can stretch to five or six; 'a couple of minutes' really means two.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a few minute'. 'A few' always takes a plural noun.

entry_json.definition: on several separate occasions, usually three to five; a vague statement of frequency
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have been to Singapore a few times for work.
example_sentences: I go swimming a few times a month, usually when the pool is quiet.
Students who retake the exam a few times usually improve their planning, not their English.

contexts.text: I have been to Singapore a few times for work.
I go swimming a few times a month, usually when the pool is quiet.
Students who retake the exam a few times usually improve their planning, not their English.

confusables.difference: 'Several times' is slightly more and sounds more formal. In writing prefer 'on several occasions'.

entry_json.avoid: Too vague for Task 1. If the chart gives a number, use the number.

entry_json.definition: a period of roughly three to five years; very common when describing change over time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have lived in this city for a few years now.
example_sentences: Rents were stable for a few years and then rose sharply after 2016.
A few years ago most people carried a camera; now the phone has replaced it.

contexts.text: I have lived in this city for a few years now.
Rents were stable for a few years and then rose sharply after 2016.
A few years ago most people carried a camera; now the phone has replaced it.

confusables.term: in a few years / for a few years
confusables.difference: 'In a few years' points forward to a moment; 'for a few years' measures a stretch of time. They are not interchangeable.

entry_json.avoid: 'A few years ago' needs the past simple: 'I moved here a few years ago', not 'I have moved'.

entry_json.definition: a sensible plan or suggestion; it usually follows 'it is' or the verb 'think'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is a good idea to walk part of the journey if you sit down all day.
example_sentences: I think studying with other people is a good idea, at least some of the time.
Charging for plastic bags seemed a good idea, and the figures suggest it worked.
collocations: it is a good idea to do sth
think it is a good idea

contexts.text: It is a good idea to walk part of the journey if you sit down all day.
I think studying with other people is a good idea, at least some of the time.
Charging for plastic bags seemed a good idea, and the figures suggest it worked.

confusables.difference: 'A nice idea' often carries an unspoken 'but it will not work'. 'A good idea' is genuine approval.

entry_json.avoid: Weak on its own in Task 2. Say why it is a good idea, or write 'an effective measure'.

entry_json.definition: a lot; it works as an adverb after a verb - 'it has changed a great deal' - or before a comparative
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Car ownership rose a great deal between 1990 and 2010.
example_sentences: Teaching methods have changed a great deal in the last ten years.
Family life has changed a great deal in a single generation.

contexts.text: Car ownership rose a great deal between 1990 and 2010.
Teaching methods have changed a great deal in the last ten years.
Family life has changed a great deal in a single generation.

confusables.difference: The same meaning in a different register. 'A lot' is spoken; 'a great deal' is its written equivalent and lifts an essay sentence.
Before a noun you must add 'of': 'a great deal of money'. On its own it follows the verb.

entry_json.avoid: It modifies verbs and comparatives, not plain adjectives. Not 'a great deal expensive'.

entry_json.definition: much better; 'a great deal' here strengthens a comparative adjective or adverb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Air quality in the city is a great deal better than it was a decade ago.
example_sentences: Students do a great deal better when they are taught in small groups.
Rail punctuality was a great deal better in the second half of the period.
collocations: a great deal better than sth

contexts.text: Air quality in the city is a great deal better than it was a decade ago.
Students do a great deal better when they are taught in small groups.
Rail punctuality was a great deal better in the second half of the period.

confusables.difference: Identical in meaning. 'A great deal better' is heavier and more formal, so do not use it twice in one paragraph.

entry_json.avoid: Only with comparatives. 'A great deal good' is wrong; it has to be 'better'.

entry_json.definition: a large amount of something uncountable; the pattern is a great deal of + uncountable noun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Commuting consumes a great deal of time that could be spent with family.
example_sentences: The study required a great deal of data collected over twenty years.
Buying a home takes a great deal of money that young people simply do not have.

contexts.text: Commuting consumes a great deal of time that could be spent with family.
The study required a great deal of data collected over twenty years.
Buying a home takes a great deal of money that young people simply do not have.

confusables.difference: 'A great deal of' goes with uncountables; 'a great many' goes with countable plurals - a great many students.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a great deal of people'. People are countable, so use 'a great many people'.

entry_json.definition: employment that lasts a whole career with one employer; it usually appears in the past or the negative, because the idea has largely disappeared
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My grandfather had a job for life; my generation changes employer every three years.
example_sentences: Nobody expects a job for life any more, and some people actually prefer it that way.
The end of a job for life has turned retraining into a lifelong task.
collocations: the end of a job for life
no longer a job for life

contexts.text: My grandfather had a job for life; my generation changes employer every three years.
Nobody expects a job for life any more, and some people actually prefer it that way.
The end of a job for life has turned retraining into a lifelong task.

confusables.difference: 'A permanent job' is a contract type you can hold today. 'A job for life' is a whole-career idea and is nearly always used to say it no longer exists.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for a contract with no end date - that is 'a permanent position'.

entry_json.definition: a type of something; in speech it also hedges, meaning 'roughly' or 'something like'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is a kind of festival that only happens in the north of the country.
example_sentences: Social media has become a kind of public square, for better or worse.
My role is a kind of bridge between the engineers and the clients.

contexts.text: It is a kind of festival that only happens in the north of the country.
Social media has become a kind of public square, for better or worse.
My role is a kind of bridge between the engineers and the clients.

confusables.difference: Without the article, 'kind of' is an adverb - 'I was kind of nervous' - and is very informal. 'A kind of' introduces a noun.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a kind of a festival'. Use one article only: 'a kind of festival'.

entry_json.definition: many; it takes a countable plural noun, and the verb that follows is normally plural
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A large number of people move to the capital every year in search of work.
example_sentences: A large number of respondents said that they preferred online lectures.
A large number of illnesses could be prevented by better diet alone.
collocations: attract a large number of sth

contexts.text: A large number of people move to the capital every year in search of work.
A large number of respondents said that they preferred online lectures.
A large number of illnesses could be prevented by better diet alone.

confusables.difference: 'Number' counts - a large number of cars. 'Amount' measures - a large amount of traffic. Mixing them is one of the commonest Task 2 errors.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a large number of information'. Uncountable nouns need 'a large amount of'.

entry_json.definition: a small amount of something uncountable, or 'slightly' before an adjective or adverb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I speak a little Spanish, enough to order food and ask directions.
example_sentences: Unemployment fell a little in the final quarter of the year.
Sleeping a little longer each night makes a measurable difference to concentration.

contexts.text: I speak a little Spanish, enough to order food and ask directions.
Unemployment fell a little in the final quarter of the year.
Sleeping a little longer each night makes a measurable difference to concentration.

confusables.difference: 'A little' means some. 'Little' on its own means almost none and is negative: 'There is little evidence' says the evidence is missing.
'A little' measures uncountables - a little water. 'A few' counts - a few bottles.

entry_json.avoid: Dropping 'a' reverses the meaning, so decide whether you mean 'some' or 'hardly any'.

entry_json.definition: slightly; a spoken softener before an adjective, or a very small quantity of something uncountable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was a little bit worried about the listening section.
example_sentences: Add a little bit of salt at the end rather than at the start.
Most people would be a little bit happier with one day less in the office.

contexts.text: I was a little bit worried about the listening section.
Add a little bit of salt at the end rather than at the start.
Most people would be a little bit happier with one day less in the office.

confusables.difference: The same meaning; 'a little bit' is gentler still. Both belong to speech.
'Slightly' is the written equivalent and is what an essay needs.

entry_json.avoid: Too informal for writing. In an essay use 'slightly'.

entry_json.definition: a small amount of assistance; 'help' is uncountable here, so it takes 'a little' and never a plural
entry_json.own_context_sentence: With a little help from my tutor I managed to finish the essay on time.
example_sentences: A little help at the right moment stops a new employee from giving up.
Older relatives often need a little help rather than full-time care.

contexts.text: With a little help from my tutor I managed to finish the essay on time.
A little help at the right moment stops a new employee from giving up.
Older relatives often need a little help rather than full-time care.

confusables.difference: 'Help' has no plural in this sense, so if you need something countable use 'a few tips' or 'a few suggestions'.

entry_json.avoid: Never make 'help' plural. 'A few helps' is not English.

entry_json.definition: a small amount of money; the tone is positive, because it says you have some
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I try to put a little money aside at the end of every month.
example_sentences: A little money spent on prevention saves a great deal on treatment later.
We had saved a little money, so we travelled by train instead of flying.

contexts.text: I try to put a little money aside at the end of every month.
A little money spent on prevention saves a great deal on treatment later.
We had saved a little money, so we travelled by train instead of flying.

confusables.difference: 'A little money' means you have some. 'Little money' means almost none: 'Little money was available for repairs'.

entry_json.avoid: Money is uncountable. Not 'a few moneys' - say 'a little money' or 'a few coins'.

entry_json.definition: slightly more; used before a comparative or before an uncountable noun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Students need a little more time to adapt than most timetables allow.
example_sentences: If people walked a little more, the health service would spend a great deal less.
Households spent a little more on housing and a little less on food.

contexts.text: Students need a little more time to adapt than most timetables allow.
If people walked a little more, the health service would spend a great deal less.
Households spent a little more on housing and a little less on food.

confusables.difference: A question of size. 'A little more' matches 'slightly' in a Task 1 description, not 'sharply'.

entry_json.avoid: With countable plurals use 'a few more': 'a few more students', not 'a little more students'.

entry_json.definition: a small amount of sugar; sugar is uncountable, so it takes 'a little' and stays singular
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I take my tea with a little sugar and no milk.
example_sentences: A little sugar in a home-cooked meal is not the problem; processed food is.
My grandmother added a little sugar to almost everything she cooked.

contexts.text: I take my tea with a little sugar and no milk.
A little sugar in a home-cooked meal is not the problem; processed food is.
My grandmother added a little sugar to almost everything she cooked.

confusables.difference: 'Two sugars' is spoken shorthand for spoonfuls in a hot drink. The substance itself stays uncountable: 'a little sugar'.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a little sugars'. Keep the noun singular.

entry_json.definition: an extended period; it follows 'for' or works as the object of verbs such as 'take' and 'spend'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have lived in the same neighbourhood for a long time.
example_sentences: Waiting a long time for treatment is what patients complain about most.
It takes a long time to build the trust a good team depends on.

contexts.text: I have lived in the same neighbourhood for a long time.
Waiting a long time for treatment is what patients complain about most.
It takes a long time to build the trust a good team depends on.

confusables.difference: Modern English needs the article: 'for a long time', not 'for long time'. 'Long time no see' is a fixed joke, not a model.

entry_json.avoid: With a present perfect it means the situation continues: 'I have known her for a long time' - she is still a friend.

entry_json.definition: far back in the past; because it fixes a finished point in time it forces the past simple
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My grandparents moved to the city a long time ago, before the motorway was built.
example_sentences: The festival began a long time ago as a celebration of the harvest.
Handwriting stopped being essential a long time ago, yet schools still test it.
collocations: that was a long time ago

contexts.text: My grandparents moved to the city a long time ago, before the motorway was built.
The festival began a long time ago as a celebration of the harvest.
Handwriting stopped being essential a long time ago, yet schools still test it.

confusables.difference: 'A long time ago' fixes a point in the past. 'For a long time' measures a stretch that may reach the present.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'I have moved here a long time ago'. A finished past time needs the past simple.

entry_json.definition: a great distance; also used figuratively in 'go a long way' (be enough, help a lot) and 'come a long way' (make great progress)
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I live quite a long way from the centre, so I cycle to the station.
example_sentences: The country has come a long way in twenty years, but rural areas still lag behind.
A small salary goes a long way in a town where rents are low.

contexts.text: I live quite a long way from the centre, so I cycle to the station.
The country has come a long way in twenty years, but rural areas still lag behind.
A small salary goes a long way in a town where rents are low.

confusables.difference: In positive statements English prefers 'a long way': 'It is a long way to the airport'. 'Far' is normal in questions and negatives.

entry_json.avoid: 'Go a long way' is about being sufficient, not about distance. Check which sense you mean.

entry_json.definition: very much, or very often; it follows the verb - 'I read a lot' - and is two words, never one
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I read a lot in the evenings, mostly online.
example_sentences: Traffic in my city has changed a lot in the last five years.
People complain a lot about hospital waiting times, and the figures support them.

contexts.text: I read a lot in the evenings, mostly online.
Traffic in my city has changed a lot in the last five years.
People complain a lot about hospital waiting times, and the figures support them.

confusables.difference: 'A lot' is the spoken form. 'Much' after a verb belongs mainly to negatives and questions: 'I do not read much'.
'A lot' is always two words. 'Alot' does not exist in English.

entry_json.avoid: Two words, always. In an essay replace it with 'considerably' or 'a great deal'.

entry_json.definition: much more; used before a comparative adjective, before a noun, or on its own after a verb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Eating out costs a lot more than it did five years ago.
example_sentences: Children today have a lot more choice and a lot more pressure.
We would need a lot more evidence before banning something outright.

contexts.text: Eating out costs a lot more than it did five years ago.
Children today have a lot more choice and a lot more pressure.
We would need a lot more evidence before banning something outright.

confusables.difference: Before countable plurals, formal writing prefers 'many more people'; 'a lot more people' is the spoken version.

entry_json.avoid: Informal. In Task 1 write 'considerably more', or simply give the figure.

entry_json.definition: a large quantity of something; unlike 'many' and 'much' it works with both countable plurals and uncountables
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I spend a lot of time revising at the weekend.
example_sentences: A lot of people are moving out of the city because of rent.
There is a lot of plastic waste on the beach at the end of summer.

contexts.text: I spend a lot of time revising at the weekend.
A lot of people are moving out of the city because of rent.
There is a lot of plastic waste on the beach at the end of summer.

confusables.difference: 'Lots of' is more informal still. Between the two, 'a lot of' is the safer spoken choice.
In an essay replace 'a lot of' with 'many' before plurals and 'a great deal of' before uncountables.

entry_json.avoid: Acceptable in Speaking, weak in Task 2. Swap it for 'a large number of' or 'a great deal of'.

entry_json.definition: many tasks to complete; note that adding 'with' changes the meaning entirely - 'have a lot to do with sth' means to be closely connected to it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I had a lot to do that week, so I turned down the invitation.
example_sentences: There is always a lot to do in the final month before exams.
Diet has a lot to do with how well people sleep.
collocations: a lot to do with sth

contexts.text: I had a lot to do that week, so I turned down the invitation.
There is always a lot to do in the final month before exams.
Diet has a lot to do with how well people sleep.

confusables.term: a lot to do with sth
confusables.difference: One preposition changes everything: without 'with' it means workload, with 'with' it means connection.

entry_json.avoid: Decide which meaning you want before you add 'with'.

entry_json.definition: a method people use to exchange information; the noun 'means' keeps its -s in the singular
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Email is still a means of communication that almost every workplace depends on.
example_sentences: The report treats social media as a means of communication rather than as entertainment.
A letter was once a means of communication everyone used; today almost nobody writes one.

contexts.text: Email is still a means of communication that almost every workplace depends on.
The report treats social media as a means of communication rather than as entertainment.
A letter was once a means of communication everyone used; today almost nobody writes one.

confusables.difference: Identical in meaning; 'a means of communication' is the academic form and lifts a Task 2 sentence.
'Means' never loses its -s, even when it is singular.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'a mean of communication'. The word is 'means' in both singular and plural.

entry_json.definition: a method or instrument for achieving something; followed by a noun or an -ing form, and 'means' is the same in singular and plural
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cycling should be treated as a means of transport, not just as a form of exercise.
example_sentences: Taxation is a means of redistributing wealth as well as of raising revenue.
Education is a means of escaping poverty, but only where the jobs exist.

contexts.text: Cycling should be treated as a means of transport, not just as a form of exercise.
Taxation is a means of redistributing wealth as well as of raising revenue.
Education is a means of escaping poverty, but only where the jobs exist.

confusables.difference: 'Method' names a procedure you follow step by step; 'means' names anything that gets you there, including a tool or a route.

entry_json.avoid: The -s belongs to the word itself: 'a means', 'two means'. Never 'a mean'.

entry_json.definition: a way of travelling or of moving goods, such as a bus, a bicycle or a train
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The survey asked respondents to name a means of transport they had used that week.
example_sentences: A means of transport that most people can afford does more for a city than a fast one that few can use.
The metro is a means of transport I rely on every single day.

contexts.text: The survey asked respondents to name a means of transport they had used that week.
A means of transport that most people can afford does more for a city than a fast one that few can use.
The metro is a means of transport I rely on every single day.

confusables.difference: Interchangeable in Task 1. 'Mode of transport' is slightly more technical and appears constantly in chart questions.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a transport means', and never 'a mean of transport'.

entry_json.definition: a very short time; a polite, deliberately vague way of asking someone to wait
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Give me a moment or two and I will find the file.
example_sentences: Take a moment or two to plan before you start writing.
A moment or two of quiet before a difficult conversation makes a real difference.

contexts.text: Give me a moment or two and I will find the file.
Take a moment or two to plan before you start writing.
A moment or two of quiet before a difficult conversation makes a real difference.

confusables.difference: Almost identical. 'A moment or two' is shorter and more polite; 'a minute or two' is closer to real measurement.

entry_json.avoid: Spoken. In writing use 'briefly' or 'for a short time'.

entry_json.definition: several; it takes a countable plural noun and, importantly, a plural verb - 'a number of factors are involved'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A number of factors explain why the policy failed in rural areas.
example_sentences: A number of countries recorded a fall in emissions after 2010.
A number of my colleagues have moved to a four-day week.

contexts.text: A number of factors explain why the policy failed in rural areas.
A number of countries recorded a fall in emissions after 2010.
A number of my colleagues have moved to a four-day week.

confusables.difference: 'A number of students were late' means several. 'The number of students was falling' talks about the figure itself and takes a singular verb.

entry_json.avoid: 'A number of' takes a plural verb. Not 'a number of factors explains'.

entry_json.definition: a length of time, usually a defined one; standard in Task 1 for saying what a chart covers
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The chart covers a period of time stretching from 1990 to 2020.
example_sentences: Habits formed over a period of time are much harder to break.
Learning a language takes a period of time that no app can shorten.

contexts.text: The chart covers a period of time stretching from 1990 to 2020.
Habits formed over a period of time are much harder to break.
Learning a language takes a period of time that no app can shorten.

confusables.difference: Both exist. 'A period of time' is the natural English phrase; 'time period' is more technical and belongs to scientific writing.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it when you can name the period. 'Between 1990 and 2020' is far stronger in Task 1.

entry_json.definition: a small amount of money, roughly one or two pounds; used to say a difference in price is trivial
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A coffee near the station costs a pound or two more than one at home.
example_sentences: Most people will pay a pound or two extra for something that lasts longer.
The market is cheaper, but only by a pound or two on a weekly shop.

contexts.text: A coffee near the station costs a pound or two more than one at home.
Most people will pay a pound or two extra for something that lasts longer.
The market is cheaper, but only by a pound or two on a weekly shop.

confusables.difference: The same money, a different point. 'A pound or two' stresses how little it is; 'a couple of pounds' simply counts.

entry_json.avoid: British currency and British speech. Keep it for Speaking, not for an essay.

entry_json.definition: a set of different things of the same type; it takes a plural noun and signals variety within limits
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Universities now offer a range of courses that can be studied entirely online.
example_sentences: The clinic treats a range of conditions linked to poor diet.
Employers want a range of skills rather than one narrow specialism.

contexts.text: Universities now offer a range of courses that can be studied entirely online.
The clinic treats a range of conditions linked to poor diet.
Employers want a range of skills rather than one narrow specialism.

confusables.difference: 'Range' suggests a planned set with two ends, like a product line or a price band. 'Variety' stresses that the things differ from each other.

entry_json.avoid: It needs a plural noun: 'a range of courses', not 'a range of course'.

vocab_new.lemma: a rise in the number of visitors

entry_json.definition: an increase in how many people visit a place; the standard Task 1 wording for a rising visitor line
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The graph shows a rise in the number of visitors to the national park after 2010.

entry_json.avoid: The preposition is 'in': a rise in the number of visitors, never 'a rise of visitors'.

entry_json.definition: several different kinds of something; it takes a countable plural noun and normally a plural verb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A healthy diet contains a variety of vegetables rather than one so-called superfood.
example_sentences: The data were collected from a variety of sources over five years.
Cities attract people because they offer a variety of ways to live.

contexts.text: A healthy diet contains a variety of vegetables rather than one so-called superfood.
The data were collected from a variety of sources over five years.
Cities attract people because they offer a variety of ways to live.

confusables.difference: 'Variety' emphasises difference; 'range' emphasises the span from one end to the other, as in a range of prices.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a variety of information'. Choose a countable plural, or write 'various kinds of information'.

entry_json.definition: a large number of different things of the same type; one of the most useful noun phrases in Task 2
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Schools should offer a wide range of subjects so that late developers are not shut out.
example_sentences: The survey covered a wide range of age groups across six regions.
A single phone now replaces a wide range of devices we used to own separately.
collocations: offer a wide range of sth
cover a wide range of sth

contexts.text: Schools should offer a wide range of subjects so that late developers are not shut out.
The survey covered a wide range of age groups across six regions.
A single phone now replaces a wide range of devices we used to own separately.

confusables.difference: Nearly identical. Use 'range' for things that sit on a scale or a list, 'variety' when you want to stress how different they are.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a wide range of choice'. The noun after it must be plural: 'a wide range of choices'.

entry_json.definition: having the skill, the chance or the permission to do something; it follows 'be' and takes a to-infinitive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: After six months I was able to follow lectures without subtitles.
example_sentences: Patients should be able to book an appointment without waiting three weeks.
Only a third of respondents were able to work from home during the period.

contexts.text: After six months I was able to follow lectures without subtitles.
Patients should be able to book an appointment without waiting three weeks.
Only a third of respondents were able to work from home during the period.

confusables.difference: 'Can' has no infinitive and no perfect form, so 'able to' fills the gaps: 'will be able to', 'has been able to'.
'Able to' takes an infinitive; 'capable of' takes -ing. Never 'capable to do'.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'able of doing'. The pattern is fixed: able to do.

entry_json.definition: most importantly of all; it singles out the strongest point in a list and usually opens a clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Above all, teachers need time to prepare, not more paperwork.
example_sentences: The policy must be affordable, practical and, above all, enforceable.
Above all, people want to feel that the work they do matters.
collocations: above all, it is important to

contexts.text: Above all, teachers need time to prepare, not more paperwork.
The policy must be affordable, practical and, above all, enforceable.
Above all, people want to feel that the work they do matters.

confusables.difference: 'First of all' orders your points; 'above all' ranks them. Only one point can be 'above all'.

entry_json.avoid: Use it once in an essay. If everything is 'above all', nothing is.

entry_json.definition: the chance or the right to use or reach something; the preposition is always 'to' and the noun is uncountable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Access to fast internet now decides which children can study at home.
example_sentences: The report measured access to clean water in twelve rural districts.
Not everyone has access to the same technology, and that gap is widening.

contexts.text: Access to fast internet now decides which children can study at home.
The report measured access to clean water in twelve rural districts.
Not everyone has access to the same technology, and that gap is widening.

confusables.difference: The preposition is 'to', never 'of': access to education.
The adjective takes a different frame: 'education should be accessible to everyone', not 'access to everyone'.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'an access'. The noun is uncountable: 'access to healthcare', not 'an access to healthcare'.

entry_json.definition: to form a stated part of a total, or to explain why something happens; in Task 1 it is the standard verb for shares of a whole, and it never splits
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Housing accounted for almost half of all household spending in 2015.
example_sentences: Transport accounts for a growing share of total emissions.
Stress accounts for a lot of the sick days that employers complain about.
collocations: account for a share of sth
account for the majority of sth

contexts.text: Housing accounted for almost half of all household spending in 2015.
Transport accounts for a growing share of total emissions.
Stress accounts for a lot of the sick days that employers complain about.

confusables.difference: Both can mean 'give a reason', but only 'account for' can express a proportion: 'accounts for 40% of the total'.
A different phrase with a different meaning: to consider something when making a decision.

entry_json.avoid: It always keeps 'for' and never separates: 'account for 30%', not 'account 30%'.

entry_json.definition: said to have done something wrong; the pattern is be accused of + noun or -ing, never a to-infinitive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Anyone accused of a crime is entitled to a fair hearing.
example_sentences: Newspapers are often accused of reporting only the most dramatic cases.
Being accused of something in public can ruin a reputation before any trial.

contexts.text: Anyone accused of a crime is entitled to a fair hearing.
Newspapers are often accused of reporting only the most dramatic cases.
Being accused of something in public can ruin a reputation before any trial.

confusables.difference: 'Accused of' can be everyday and social. 'Charged with' is the formal legal step taken by the police.
'Blamed for' points at a result - blamed for the delay. 'Accused of' points at an act - accused of stealing.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'accused to steal'. The pattern is 'accused of stealing'.

entry_json.definition: to perform the function of something without necessarily being it; very common in academic description, and it keeps the article: act as a barrier
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Trees in a city act as a natural filter for polluted air.
example_sentences: The membrane acts as a barrier between the two solutions.
A good manager acts as a shield between the team and the pressure from above.

contexts.text: Trees in a city act as a natural filter for polluted air.
The membrane acts as a barrier between the two solutions.
A good manager acts as a shield between the team and the pressure from above.

confusables.difference: 'Act as' states a function. 'Act like' describes behaviour that resembles something: 'He acts like a child'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the article: 'act as a filter', not 'act as filter'.

entry_json.definition: to make something greater, usually a problem, a cost or a feeling; note that it has no object of its own, unlike 'add sth to sth'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: New office towers add to the traffic that the city already cannot handle.
example_sentences: Rising fuel prices added to the cost of every item on the shelf.
Long shifts add to the stress that nurses already carry.

contexts.text: New office towers add to the traffic that the city already cannot handle.
Rising fuel prices added to the cost of every item on the shelf.
Long shifts add to the stress that nurses already carry.

confusables.difference: 'Add to sth' means the subject increases something. 'Add sth to sth' moves one thing into another: 'Add sugar to the mixture'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for physically putting something somewhere - that needs 'add sth to sth'.

entry_json.definition: either 'remember, this is the reason' when you give support the reader half knows, or 'in the end, contrary to expectation' at the end of a clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Students should be consulted; after all, it is their time that is being spent.
example_sentences: The meeting was cancelled, so I got an early night after all.
Cheap flights are not really cheap after all, once you add the extras.

contexts.text: Students should be consulted; after all, it is their time that is being spent.
The meeting was cancelled, so I got an early night after all.
Cheap flights are not really cheap after all, once you add the extras.

confusables.difference: 'At last' expresses relief after waiting. 'After all' either supplies a reason or reverses an expectation.
'Finally' orders events in a sequence. 'After all' never does.

entry_json.avoid: It does not mean 'finally'. Never use it to introduce the last paragraph of an essay.

entry_json.definition: repeatedly, usually with a note of frustration; it sits after the verb or at the end of the clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The same mistakes appear again and again in student writing.
example_sentences: I had to explain the system again and again until everyone understood it.
Governments promise action again and again, and emissions keep rising.

contexts.text: The same mistakes appear again and again in student writing.
I had to explain the system again and again until everyone understood it.
Governments promise action again and again, and emissions keep rising.

confusables.difference: The same meaning, slightly more formal and shorter.
Very close, but more spoken, and it usually adds 'again' at the end.

entry_json.avoid: It carries impatience. Do not use it for something you enjoy repeating.

entry_json.definition: to have the same opinion as someone; with a person or an opinion the preposition is 'with', and the two words never separate
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I agree with people who say exams measure memory more than ability.
example_sentences: Most researchers agree with the view that screens before bed harm sleep.
My brother and I rarely agree with each other about politics.
collocations: could not agree with sb more

contexts.text: I agree with people who say exams measure memory more than ability.
Most researchers agree with the view that screens before bed harm sleep.
My brother and I rarely agree with each other about politics.

confusables.difference: 'Agree with' is about opinions; 'agree to' is about accepting a proposal: 'They agreed to the plan'.
'Agree on' means two sides reach a shared decision: 'They agreed on a date'.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'I am agree'. 'Agree' is a full verb, so it is simply 'I agree'.

entry_json.definition: to intend to achieve something; it takes a to-infinitive and is the natural verb for stating the purpose of a policy
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The scheme aims to cut car journeys in the centre by a third.
example_sentences: The study aimed to measure how students use online libraries.
I aim to finish the report before the end of the week.

contexts.text: The scheme aims to cut car journeys in the centre by a third.
The study aimed to measure how students use online libraries.
I aim to finish the report before the end of the week.

confusables.difference: Both exist. 'Aim to do' takes a person or an organisation as subject; 'aimed at doing' hangs off a noun such as campaign or policy.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'aim to reducing'. After 'aim to' use the bare infinitive.

entry_json.definition: designed to achieve something; a participle phrase that follows a noun such as policy, campaign or measure, and the verb after 'at' must take -ing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A campaign aimed at reducing sugar consumption cut sales within a year.
example_sentences: The programme is aimed at raising literacy among adults who left school early.
Taxes aimed at discouraging plastic packaging work better than appeals to conscience.
collocations: a policy aimed at doing sth
a campaign aimed at doing sth

contexts.text: A campaign aimed at reducing sugar consumption cut sales within a year.
The programme is aimed at raising literacy among adults who left school early.
Taxes aimed at discouraging plastic packaging work better than appeals to conscience.

confusables.difference: 'Aim to do' needs a subject that intends something. 'Aimed at doing' attaches straight to a noun and needs none.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'aimed at reduce'. After the preposition 'at' the verb takes -ing.

entry_json.definition: intended for a particular group of people; used of advertising, courses and policies to name their audience
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Advertising aimed at children should be restricted during school hours.
example_sentences: The course is aimed at students who have never studied statistics.
Loans aimed at young people often hide the real cost in the small print.

contexts.text: Advertising aimed at children should be restricted during school hours.
The course is aimed at students who have never studied statistics.
Loans aimed at young people often hide the real cost in the small print.

confusables.difference: With a person it names the audience; with an -ing form it names the purpose. Compare 'aimed at children' and 'aimed at protecting children'.

entry_json.avoid: 'Aimed at' takes a target group, not a place. Not 'a course aimed at London'.

entry_json.definition: concerned entirely with something; 'it is all about X' claims that X is what really matters
entry_json.own_context_sentence: For a lot of employers, hiring is all about attitude rather than qualifications.
example_sentences: The course was all about learning to argue, not about learning facts.
Success in sport is all about consistency over years, not one good season.

contexts.text: For a lot of employers, hiring is all about attitude rather than qualifications.
The course was all about learning to argue, not about learning facts.
Success in sport is all about consistency over years, not one good season.

confusables.difference: 'About' simply names the topic. 'All about' insists it is the only thing that counts, which is an opinion, not a description.

entry_json.avoid: Spoken emphasis. In an essay write 'depends primarily on'.

entry_json.definition: two senses: almost or very nearly, before a strong adjective or participle ('all but impossible'), and everyone or everything except, before a noun or number
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Coal has all but disappeared from the country's electricity supply.
example_sentences: All but two of the regions recorded a fall in unemployment.
Paper maps have all but vanished from everyday life.

contexts.text: Coal has all but disappeared from the country's electricity supply.
All but two of the regions recorded a fall in unemployment.
Paper maps have all but vanished from everyday life.
