'As at' is an accounting form used for balances on a particular date; 'as of' is the general one.

entry_json.avoid: Formal and written. In Speaking say 'from January' instead.

entry_json.definition: rather than; it marks a deliberate contrast between two options and takes a noun or an -ing form after it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The debate is really about teaching skills as opposed to teaching facts.
example_sentences: Sixty per cent travelled by train, as opposed to twenty per cent by car.
Treating illness as opposed to preventing it is what makes health systems so expensive.
collocations: as opposed to simply doing sth

contexts.text: The debate is really about teaching skills as opposed to teaching facts.
Sixty per cent travelled by train, as opposed to twenty per cent by car.
Treating illness as opposed to preventing it is what makes health systems so expensive.

confusables.difference: Interchangeable, but 'rather than' is lighter and can take a bare infinitive; 'as opposed to' always takes a noun or -ing.
On its own, 'opposed to' means 'against': 'The council is opposed to the plan'.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'as opposed to teach'. After 'to' here the verb takes -ing.

entry_json.definition: working together with other people rather than alone; a standard collocation in job advertisements and in Speaking about work
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I enjoy working as part of a team more than working on my own.
example_sentences: Skills learned as part of a team transfer to almost any workplace.
Group projects teach students to think as part of a team, which examinations never do.
collocations: work as part of a team
as part of a small team
function as part of a team

contexts.text: I enjoy working as part of a team more than working on my own.
Skills learned as part of a team transfer to almost any workplace.
Group projects teach students to think as part of a team, which examinations never do.

confusables.difference: Both are used, but 'as part of a team' is the fixed collocation in job advertisements and CVs.
'As a team' means the whole group acts together; 'as part of a team' is about your own role inside it.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the article: 'as part of a team', not 'as part of team'.

entry_json.definition: as one element inside something larger; it links an action to the plan or process it belongs to, and takes no article after 'as'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The tax was introduced as part of a wider plan to cut car use.
example_sentences: Students completed the questionnaire as part of their normal timetable.
Exercise works best as part of a routine rather than as an occasional effort.

contexts.text: The tax was introduced as part of a wider plan to cut car use.
Students completed the questionnaire as part of their normal timetable.
Exercise works best as part of a routine rather than as an occasional effort.

confusables.difference: With the article it is an ordinary noun phrase: 'that is a part of the problem'. Without it, 'as part of' is a link.
One space changes everything: 'apart from' means 'except for'.

entry_json.avoid: No article after 'as': 'as part of a plan', not 'as a part of a plan'.

entry_json.definition: immediately after; it introduces a time clause, and for future meaning the verb inside it stays present
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I will send the file as soon as I get back to my desk.
example_sentences: Patients recover faster when treatment begins as soon as the first symptoms appear.
I check my email as soon as I wake up, which is probably a bad habit.

contexts.text: I will send the file as soon as I get back to my desk.
Patients recover faster when treatment begins as soon as the first symptoms appear.
I check my email as soon as I wake up, which is probably a bad habit.

confusables.difference: 'When' is neutral about the gap between the two events; 'as soon as' insists there is none.
'Once' is close in meaning and slightly more formal: 'once the results are published'.

entry_json.avoid: No future tense in the clause: 'as soon as I arrive', not 'as soon as I will arrive'.

entry_json.definition: at the earliest opportunity; a fixed phrase, very common in emails, letters and requests
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Please let me know as soon as possible whether the date suits you.
example_sentences: People should see a doctor as soon as possible rather than waiting for it to pass.
Feedback helps most when students receive it as soon as possible after the test.
collocations: as soon as possible after sth

contexts.text: Please let me know as soon as possible whether the date suits you.
People should see a doctor as soon as possible rather than waiting for it to pass.
Feedback helps most when students receive it as soon as possible after the test.

confusables.difference: Softer and more personal; 'as soon as possible' can sound like an instruction.
'Immediately' allows no delay at all; 'as soon as possible' accepts that there may be one.

entry_json.avoid: Write it out in full in a formal letter. 'ASAP' is too abrupt for Task 1 General.

entry_json.definition: either 'in the strict sense of the word', usually inside a negative, or 'therefore', linking a consequence to a quality just described
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is no entrance examination as such, only an interview.
example_sentences: It is not a promotion as such, but the work is far more interesting.
The country has few natural resources; as such, it has had to build an economy on services.

contexts.text: There is no entrance examination as such, only an interview.
It is not a promotion as such, but the work is far more interesting.
The country has few natural resources; as such, it has had to build an economy on services.

confusables.difference: Reversing the words reverses the job: 'such as' introduces examples, 'as such' never does.
Close in the second sense, but 'as such' should refer back to a described quality, not to any previous idea at all.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse it with 'such as'. Examples always need 'such as'.

entry_json.definition: as if; it introduces an imagined or untrue comparison, and an unreal one takes a past tense
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The report was written as though the reader already knew the background.
example_sentences: The line rises as though the trend would continue for ever, which it did not.
Grandparents are often treated as though they had nothing left to teach.

contexts.text: The report was written as though the reader already knew the background.
The line rises as though the trend would continue for ever, which it did not.
Grandparents are often treated as though they had nothing left to teach.

confusables.difference: No difference in meaning. 'As though' is a shade more formal, so it suits Task 2 slightly better.
A different word doing a different job: 'although' concedes a fact, 'as though' compares with something imagined.

entry_json.avoid: For an unreal comparison use the past: 'as though they had', not 'as though they have'.

entry_json.definition: about how; a formal link used after nouns of doubt or disagreement such as question, debate, guidance and view
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is little agreement as to how quickly the technology should be regulated.
example_sentences: The report offers no guidance as to how the figures were collected.
Opinions differ as to how much difference individual action really makes.

contexts.text: There is little agreement as to how quickly the technology should be regulated.
The report offers no guidance as to how the figures were collected.
Opinions differ as to how much difference individual action really makes.

confusables.difference: 'About how' is the everyday form; 'as to how' is formal and belongs to academic writing.
Not English. The phrase needs 'to': as to how.

entry_json.avoid: Formal. In Speaking, 'about how' sounds far more natural.

entry_json.definition: about or concerning; a formal preposition that normally follows an abstract noun such as doubt, question, decision or disagreement
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is real doubt as to the fairness of automatic sentencing.
example_sentences: The paper makes no claim as to the cause of the fall after 2010.
There is still no agreement as to the effect of screens on very young children.

contexts.text: There is real doubt as to the fairness of automatic sentencing.
The paper makes no claim as to the cause of the fall after 2010.
There is still no agreement as to the effect of screens on very young children.

confusables.difference: 'About' is neutral and everyday; 'as to' is formal and normally follows an abstract noun.
'As for' turns to a new topic; 'as to' introduces the content of a doubt or a question.

entry_json.avoid: It follows a noun, not a verb. Not 'they discussed as to the cause'.

entry_json.definition: about whether; the formal way to attach an indirect yes-or-no question to a noun such as debate, doubt or question
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The debate as to whether homework helps younger children is far from settled.
example_sentences: The study reaches no conclusion as to whether the drug shortens recovery.
There is still argument as to whether recycling actually reduces waste.

contexts.text: The debate as to whether homework helps younger children is far from settled.
The study reaches no conclusion as to whether the drug shortens recovery.
There is still argument as to whether recycling actually reduces waste.

confusables.difference: 'Whether' alone is enough after a verb: 'They discussed whether…'. 'As to whether' follows a noun.
Not used. After 'as to' the word is 'whether', never 'if'.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'as to if'. Only 'as to whether'.

entry_json.definition: also, too; it sits at the end of the clause and can never begin a sentence
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We visited the old town and the harbour as well.
example_sentences: Schools should teach personal finance as well, not only academic subjects.
Employers want experience, and increasingly they want digital skills as well.

contexts.text: We visited the old town and the harbour as well.
Schools should teach personal finance as well, not only academic subjects.
Employers want experience, and increasingly they want digital skills as well.

confusables.difference: Interchangeable at the end of a clause; 'as well' is a little more British.
'Also' goes before the main verb; 'as well' goes at the end. Not 'As well, schools should…'

entry_json.avoid: It cannot open a sentence. Use 'In addition' or 'Moreover' there.

entry_json.definition: in addition to; a verb after it takes the -ing form, and the main verb agrees with the first subject only
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Universities now teach study skills as well as subject content.
example_sentences: The clinic treats adults as well as children.
Employers look at attitude as well as qualifications.

contexts.text: Universities now teach study skills as well as subject content.
The clinic treats adults as well as children.
Employers look at attitude as well as qualifications.

confusables.difference: 'And' balances two items equally; 'as well as' makes the second one extra, and the verb still agrees with the first.
Without a following noun, 'as well' simply means 'too' and closes the clause.

entry_json.avoid: A verb after it takes -ing: 'as well as teaching', not 'as well as teach'.

entry_json.definition: to say that you want something to be given to you; 'for' is compulsory before the thing you want
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I asked for a day off and my manager agreed immediately.
example_sentences: Students rarely ask for help until the problem has become serious.
It is still difficult for many people to ask for a pay rise.

contexts.text: I asked for a day off and my manager agreed immediately.
Students rarely ask for help until the problem has become serious.
It is still difficult for many people to ask for a pay rise.

confusables.difference: Without 'for' the verb takes a question: 'I asked her the time'. With 'for' it takes the thing you want.
When you want a person to act, use 'ask sb to do sth', not 'ask for'.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'ask for to help me'. If a person is to act, use 'ask sb to do sth'.

entry_json.definition: connected with a particular activity, most often a risk or a cost; the preposition 'with' forces the -ing form
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The risks associated with sitting for long periods are now well documented.
example_sentences: The costs associated with storing renewable energy have fallen sharply.
The stress associated with buying a first home puts a lot of people off entirely.
collocations: the risks associated with doing sth
the costs associated with doing sth

contexts.text: The risks associated with sitting for long periods are now well documented.
The costs associated with storing renewable energy have fallen sharply.
The stress associated with buying a first home puts a lot of people off entirely.

confusables.difference: With a noun it names a thing; with -ing it names an activity: 'risks associated with smoking'.
'Linked to' hints at a causal chain; 'associated with' is deliberately weaker and claims no cause.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'associated with sit'. After 'with' the verb must take -ing.

entry_json.definition: connected with something, without claiming that one causes the other; standard hedging language in academic writing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Higher income is associated with longer life, although the reason is disputed.
example_sentences: Regular attendance was associated with better results across all three schools.
Certain foods are associated with festivals rather than with everyday meals.

contexts.text: Higher income is associated with longer life, although the reason is disputed.
Regular attendance was associated with better results across all three schools.
Certain foods are associated with festivals rather than with everyday meals.

confusables.difference: 'Associated with' claims only that two things occur together; 'caused by' claims a cause. Examiners notice which one you chose.
The preposition is 'with', never 'to'.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'associated to'. And do not reach for it when you actually mean 'caused by'.

entry_json.definition: in the beginning, before something changed; it sets up a contrast, so a later 'but' or 'then' is expected
entry_json.own_context_sentence: At first I found the lectures impossible to follow, but by December I was fine.
example_sentences: At first the figure fell slowly, and then it dropped sharply after 2010.
At first people liked working from home; after a year many wanted the office back.

contexts.text: At first I found the lectures impossible to follow, but by December I was fine.
At first the figure fell slowly, and then it dropped sharply after 2010.
At first people liked working from home; after a year many wanted the office back.

confusables.difference: 'First' orders steps in a list. 'At first' contrasts an early stage with a later change.
'Firstly' introduces the first point of an argument, not the first stage in time.

entry_json.avoid: It promises a change. If nothing changes later in the sentence, it sounds unfinished.

entry_json.definition: in your own house, or where you live; it takes no article, unlike 'at the home', which means a care home
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I usually eat at home during the week and go out at the weekend.
example_sentences: Working at home saves commuting time but blurs the line between work and rest.
Children who have somewhere quiet at home do far better at school.

contexts.text: I usually eat at home during the week and go out at the weekend.
Working at home saves commuting time but blurs the line between work and rest.
Children who have somewhere quiet at home do far better at school.

confusables.difference: 'At the home' means a care home or a children's home. Your own house is simply 'at home'.
'In the house' is about being physically inside the building; 'at home' is about being where you live.

entry_json.avoid: No article and no substitute preposition: 'at home', never 'in home' or 'at the home'.

entry_json.definition: finally, after a long or frustrating wait; it carries relief, so it does not fit neutral reporting
entry_json.own_context_sentence: After three attempts I passed the test at last.
example_sentences: At last the council has agreed to build on land it has owned for a decade.
When the waiting list moved at last, the patient had already been ill for a year.

contexts.text: After three attempts I passed the test at last.
At last the council has agreed to build on land it has owned for a decade.
When the waiting list moved at last, the patient had already been ill for a year.

confusables.difference: 'Finally' simply orders events; 'at last' adds relief that the wait is over.
'Lastly' introduces your final point in an essay and has nothing to do with waiting.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it to introduce your last paragraph. That is 'lastly' or 'finally'.

entry_json.definition: not less than a stated amount; it also adds a redeeming point after a negative one - 'the pay was poor, but at least…'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Adults should manage at least thirty minutes of activity a day.
example_sentences: At least half of all households owned two cars by the end of the period.
The pay was poor, but at least the hours were predictable.

contexts.text: Adults should manage at least thirty minutes of activity a day.
At least half of all households owned two cars by the end of the period.
The pay was poor, but at least the hours were predictable.

confusables.difference: The opposite direction: 'at least ten' is ten or more; 'at most ten' is ten or fewer.
One letter apart and entirely different: 'at last' means finally.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse it with 'at last'. The two are unrelated.

entry_json.definition: immediately, or simultaneously; the verb usually decides which of the two senses is meant
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Symptoms of this kind should be reported at once rather than monitored at home.
example_sentences: My manager asked me to deal with three things at once, which never works.
Trying to do several tasks at once makes every one of them slower.

contexts.text: Symptoms of this kind should be reported at once rather than monitored at home.
My manager asked me to deal with three things at once, which never works.
Trying to do several tasks at once makes every one of them slower.

confusables.difference: Identical in the first sense, and it cannot be misread. Prefer it when clarity matters.
That has only the simultaneous meaning, so it removes the ambiguity of 'at once'.

entry_json.avoid: It has two meanings. If a sentence allows both, write 'immediately' or 'simultaneously' instead.

entry_json.definition: now, at this moment in time; the written equivalent of 'at the moment', and it takes a present tense
entry_json.own_context_sentence: At present there is no tax on aviation fuel in most countries.
example_sentences: At present the technology is too expensive for widespread use.
At present I am working on two projects at the same time.

contexts.text: At present there is no tax on aviation fuel in most countries.
At present the technology is too expensive for widespread use.
At present I am working on two projects at the same time.

confusables.difference: The same meaning; 'at the moment' belongs to speech, 'at present' to writing.
In British English 'presently' usually means 'soon', not 'now', so it is a trap.

entry_json.avoid: It takes a present tense. Not 'at present the figure rose'.

entry_json.definition: in danger of harm or loss; it takes 'of' for what might happen and 'from' for what causes it, and there is no article
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Children in overcrowded housing are at risk of long-term breathing problems.
example_sentences: Around a third of the coastline is at risk from rising sea levels.
Older workers feel most at risk when a company starts to automate.

contexts.text: Children in overcrowded housing are at risk of long-term breathing problems.
Around a third of the coastline is at risk from rising sea levels.
Older workers feel most at risk when a company starts to automate.

confusables.difference: Interchangeable, but 'at risk' is the standard term in health, policy and academic writing.

confusables.term: at risk of / at risk from
confusables.difference: 'Of' introduces the outcome feared; 'from' introduces its source.

entry_json.avoid: No article: 'at risk', not 'at a risk'.

entry_json.definition: attending school as a pupil; British English drops the article, so 'at the school' means the building instead
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I studied French at school but I have forgotten most of it.
example_sentences: Children who are happy at school miss fewer days and learn more.
Both my sisters are still at school, so the house is quiet in the daytime.

contexts.text: I studied French at school but I have forgotten most of it.
Children who are happy at school miss fewer days and learn more.
Both my sisters are still at school, so the house is quiet in the daytime.

confusables.difference: 'At the school' means at that particular building, perhaps as a visitor. 'At school' means as a pupil.
American English prefers 'in school'; British English uses 'at school'.

entry_json.avoid: No article in British English, unless you really mean one specific building.

entry_json.definition: at a time you cannot or do not want to specify; it can look forward or back
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Almost everyone changes career at some point now.
example_sentences: At some point the cost of storage will fall far enough for this to become normal.
At some point during the second year I realised I had chosen the wrong subject.
collocations: at some point in the future

contexts.text: Almost everyone changes career at some point now.
At some point the cost of storage will fall far enough for this to become normal.
At some point during the second year I realised I had chosen the wrong subject.

confusables.difference: 'At one point' looks back at a specific past moment you could name; 'at some point' deliberately leaves it open.
One word, and more informal, but the same idea of an unspecified time.

entry_json.avoid: Vague by design. Never use it in Task 1, where you should give the year.

entry_json.definition: at that moment in the past; it points back at a time the reader already knows about
entry_json.own_context_sentence: At that time, fewer than one household in ten had access to the internet.
example_sentences: At that time, leaving your home town for work was still unusual.
At that time my parents were both working nights.

contexts.text: At that time, fewer than one household in ten had access to the internet.
At that time, leaving your home town for work was still unusual.
At that time my parents were both working nights.

confusables.difference: 'At the time' can rely on context alone; 'at that time' points back at a time already named.
'At this time' means now, or the present moment of a narrative.

entry_json.avoid: It needs a previously mentioned time, or the reader cannot tell which time you mean.

entry_json.definition: when someone was a particular age; the standard way to give an age in a report or a life story
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Children in Finland start formal school at the age of seven.
example_sentences: My grandfather left school at the age of fourteen to work on the farm.
Screening currently begins at the age of fifty in most regions.

contexts.text: Children in Finland start formal school at the age of seven.
My grandfather left school at the age of fourteen to work on the farm.
Screening currently begins at the age of fifty in most regions.

confusables.difference: Entirely different: 'in the age of the internet' means in that era.
'Aged fourteen' is shorter and very common in written reports.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'at the age of fourteen years old'. Use one or the other, never both.

entry_json.definition: in the first part of a named period, text or process; with 'of' the preposition must be 'at'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: At the beginning of the period, exports and imports were almost equal.
example_sentences: At the beginning of the course I could barely understand the reading list.
Habits formed at the beginning of a career tend to last for decades.
collocations: at the beginning of the year
at the beginning of the century
right at the beginning of sth

contexts.text: At the beginning of the period, exports and imports were almost equal.
At the beginning of the course I could barely understand the reading list.
Habits formed at the beginning of a career tend to last for decades.

confusables.difference: 'In the beginning' stands alone and tells a story; 'at the beginning of' points at the start of a named thing.
Interchangeable, with 'start' slightly less formal.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the beginning of the year'. Once you add 'of', the preposition is 'at'.

entry_json.definition: in the final part, when what you are referring to is already obvious from the context
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We were exhausted at the end, but the walk was worth it.
example_sentences: The two lines meet again at the end, at just under forty per cent.
There is a short written test at the end, and nothing else counts.

contexts.text: We were exhausted at the end, but the walk was worth it.
The two lines meet again at the end, at just under forty per cent.
There is a short written test at the end, and nothing else counts.

confusables.difference: As soon as you name the thing you must add 'of': 'at the end of the film'.
'In the end' means 'finally, after everything' and is about outcome, not position.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it to mean 'finally'. That is 'in the end'.

entry_json.definition: in the final part of a named period, place or process
entry_json.own_context_sentence: At the end of the period, unemployment stood at four per cent.
example_sentences: There is a small park at the end of my street.
Students who are assessed only at the end of the year learn to revise, not to think.
collocations: at the end of the year
at the end of the process
at the end of the street

contexts.text: At the end of the period, unemployment stood at four per cent.
There is a small park at the end of my street.
Students who are assessed only at the end of the year learn to revise, not to think.

confusables.difference: 'In the end' is about outcome; 'at the end of' is about position in time or space.
'By the end of' means at or before that point, and it looks at change accumulated up to then.

entry_json.avoid: The preposition is 'at', not 'in': 'at the end of the month'.

entry_json.definition: causing harm or loss to somebody or something else; it names what was sacrificed for a gain
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Economic growth has often been achieved at the expense of the environment.

Waiting times fell, but at the expense of routine operations.
Some people build a career at the expense of every relationship they have.

confusables.difference: 'At my expense' means either 'paid for by me' or 'making a joke about me'. 'At the expense of' names a sacrifice.

entry_json.definition: caused by the actions of a particular person or group; it is used almost exclusively of harm and defeat
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Victims who suffer at the hands of people they know rarely report it.

The team lost three times at the hands of the same opponent.
collocations: suffer at the hands of sb
defeat at the hands of sb
die at the hands of sb

contexts.text: Victims who suffer at the hands of people they know rarely report it.
Local newspapers have suffered at the hands of the platforms that now carry their stories.
The team lost three times at the hands of the same opponent.

confusables.difference: 'By' is neutral: 'defeated by the team'. 'At the hands of' adds that the experience was painful or unjust.
'Because of' gives a cause; 'at the hands of' names an agent who did it directly.

entry_json.avoid: Only for harm. 'Helped at the hands of a teacher' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: now, at this point in time; it goes with a present tense, most often the present continuous
entry_json.own_context_sentence: At the moment I am working part-time while I finish my degree.
example_sentences: Rents in my city are rising very fast at the moment.
At the moment there is no simple way to check where an image came from.

contexts.text: At the moment I am working part-time while I finish my degree.
Rents in my city are rising very fast at the moment.
At the moment there is no simple way to check where an image came from.

confusables.difference: The written equivalent. In Task 2 write 'at present' or 'currently'.
'In a moment' means very soon, not now.

entry_json.avoid: It takes a present tense. Not 'at the moment I worked'.

entry_json.definition: simultaneously; it also works as a discourse marker meaning 'however', introducing a qualification to what you have just said
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Technology makes learning cheaper; at the same time, it widens the gap between rich and poor students.

Emissions fell, while at the same time the economy continued to grow.
collocations: do two things at the same time

contexts.text: Technology makes learning cheaper; at the same time, it widens the gap between rich and poor students.
I was studying and working at the same time, which I would not recommend.
Emissions fell, while at the same time the economy continued to grow.
